items.title: Mike Gansey reflects on Sixers' whirlwind offseason: ‘It's just crazy in this NBA'
items.content:
Mike Gansey reflects on Sixers' whirlwind offseason: ‘It's just crazy in this NBA'  originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Mike Gansey had high ambitions entering his first offseason as the Sixers’ president of basketball operations.

By his own admission, however, there was no surefire master plan to first trade for All-NBA wing Jaylen Brown and then sign all-time great LeBron James on a veteran’s minimum salary. 

“I didn’t know how it was going to go,” Gansey said Thursday after Brown’s introductory Sixers press conference. “(James) obviously had a lot of great options. I didn’t know what he was going to decide. But I thought maybe after Jaylen, we had a better chance. I guess that was all we needed. 

“And our players were obviously the biggest recruiters. … Our ownership is obviously great with that as well. I think after the Jaylen (trade), I don’t want to say it got real, but at least we had a chance to be in the mix.”

James wound up choosing the Sixers over a group of teams that included the Cavs, Heat and Warriors. The 22-time All-Star has inked a two-year contract with a player option in the second season.

Gansey was glad to pounce on his opportunities to assemble a star-filled lineup. He noted that the Sixers now have two former NBA Finals MVPs (Brown and James) and two former regular-season MVPs (Joel Embiid and James). 

“It’s just crazy in this NBA,” he said. “You don’t know what’s going to happen. For me, it’s just, ‘Hey, I’m going to pick up the phone. I’m going to try to get involved in everything I possibly can.’ See what’s out there and be aggressive and be creative. Fortunately for us, this is where we landed.”

While Gansey is eager to watch the Sixers in action, he highlighted that the team is 0-0 and will require time to gel. Brown struck similar notes in his press conference.

“I’ve been around a long time,” Brown said, “long enough to know that what you have on paper doesn’t really mean (anything). It can if you put the work in, but if you allow distractions, if you allow the media to get into your locker room, if you allow certain things and the personalities don’t work, it could be a detriment. 

“So I’m aware that it could go either way. It just takes an amount of work, and the transparency and leadership can really guide this thing or not.”

Gansey still clearly has valid reasons to believe that the 2026-27 Sixers have enormous potential. 

“I think we have great (top-end) talent,” he said, “but also getting Anfernee Simons, Dean Wade, (Ariel) Hukporti, having Dominick Barlow, getting Labaron (Philon Jr.) in the draft. I’m just excited to see how it looks — the combinations, the lineups, the versatility we have. When you have the talent, it’s exciting, and then trying to figure it out is the hard part. But I’m excited to see what’s ahead.” 

Gansey also views Embiid’s summer as a major source of optimism.

items.title: Lakers got the offensive fit at center they desperately needed in Walker Kessler
items.content:
PHOENIX, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 31: Walker Kessler #24 of the Utah Jazz handles the ball during the first half of the Emirates NBA Cup game against the Phoenix Suns at Mortgage Matchup Center on October 31, 2025 in Phoenix, Arizona. The Suns defeated the Jazz 118-96. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Kelsey Grant/Getty Images) | Getty Images	Entering a pressure-packed summer, the entire NBA world knew the Lakers needed an upgrade at center. After a few iterations of stopgap players and rumors of who would be the perfect big man to pair with their superstar, the team landed their guy on July 1.

​LA forked over two first-round picks and two swaps to the Utah Jazz for the just turned 25-year-old Walker Kessler. Known primarily as an elite defensive anchor, the 7’2” five-man brings a level of stability and structure to an offense fully leaning into its explosive backcourt.

Today’s NBA is full of pick-and-roll maestros with Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves leading the charge as a duo in total possessions. Both operate at high volume while staying uber-efficient, placing in the 90th and 81st percentiles, respectively. The productive on-ball guards are now set to receive a dangerous dance partner.

The foundation sits on Kessler’s wide base as an excellent screener, making it difficult for defenders to chase around his frame. He blends size with superior feel. Once his primary defender is initiated with the guard, he zips to the rim or open area.

In the clip shown below, he sets up for a dribble handoff with his now fellow Laker teammate Collin Sexton. The on-ball pick obliterates his defender, rendering him completely helpless in the play. He dives in line with his ball handler to collect a bounce pass, leading to the finish at the rim.

Kessler possesses a good understanding of when to set or slip the screen early. The Auburn product leverages his spatial awareness to sneak behind unsuspecting help defenders, commonly finishing with reverse dunks under the rim.

He’s a massive, unmissable target, serving as a useful release valve when guards find themselves in trouble. When he’s not an on-ball screener, he parks himself around the dunker spot and must be accounted for.

​During his latest healthy year in the 2024-25 season, Kessler finished 73.6% of his attempts in the restricted area. That ranked sixth among all centers who attempted at least five per game, ahead of players like Jalen Duren and even Nikola Jokić.

Kessler doesn’t possess the same quick-twitch trampoline as the prototypical lob threats, but is effective nonetheless as a vertical spacer. His 9’5” standing reach means his catch radius is infinite. What seem to be dangerous lobs like the one below from near half court are in his wheelhouse where a back screen creates a second of indecision, opening up the alley-oop.

items.title: Former Warriors guard Monta Ellis named general manager of Alcorn State's men's basketball team
items.content:
In an effort to turn around its men's basketball program, Alcorn State is turning to someone with a lengthy history of professional experience. Former Golden State Warriors guard — and 12-year NBA veteran — Monta Ellis was named the team's new general manager Friday, Alcorn State announced. 

Ellis, 40, last played in the NBA during the 2016-17 season. 

Former Warriors and Mavericks guard Monta Ellis is the new GM for the men’s basketball program at Alcorn State (@BRAVESSPORTS): pic.twitter.com/xPMBBuh90D

— Marc Stein (@TheSteinLine) August 7, 2026Since his playing days, Ellis has focused on his family, per ESPN. His son, Monta Ellis Jr., is a 2028 recruit, and Monta Sr. said he's been guiding his son through that experience. 

While Ellis doesn't have experience as a general manager, he did mention he's coached and trained kids over the past decade, per ESPN.

"I've been coaching and training kids for the last 10 years, and I've seen a lot of kids that could play and didn't get scholarships. I just think it's an opportunity for kids like that and also to give back to the state of Mississippi, trying to bring a lot of in-state kids to keep them at home versus letting them go out of state and to other colleges."

Ellis also doesn't have college experience. Back when he was an NBA prospect, players were allowed to forego college and go right to the NBA. Ellis took that path, and was selected by the Warriors in the second round of the 2005 NBA Draft.

He spent his first six-and-a-half seasons in the NBA with Golden State, winning the Most-Improved Player award during the 2006-07 season. 

Ellis was eventually traded to the Milwaukee Bucks, where he spent a season-and-a-half before hitting the free-agent market. He then spent two years with the Dallas Mavericks and one year with the Indiana Pacers before he was waived in 2017.

Over his 12-year NBA career, Ellis averaged 17.8 points and 4.6 assists per game. 

Alcorn State, an HBCU, is looking for stability after its men's basketball team posted three straight seasons with a record under .500. E. D'Wayne Robinson, Alcorn State's athletic director, said Ellis' presence gives the school credibility and is similar to an endorsement, per ESPN.

"It's almost like an endorsement from someone that endorses a brand product," Robinson said. "There are certain people out there that it raises the level of respect for that product. And with Monta having the type of gravitas that he has from being a player — he's been a good guy over the years — the program benefits from his brand."

Ellis should, at least, have some familiarity with Alcorn State. He grew up in Mississippi and attended Lanier High School, roughly a 90 minute drive from Alcorn State, which is located near Lorman, Mississippi.

items.title: What Dillon Brooks' $73 million extension means for Phoenix's future
items.content:
When news broke earlier this week of Dillon Brooks’ three-year, $73 million extension to stay in Phoenix, I’d imagine a decent subsection of the basketball consortium scratched its collective head in confusion. 

Not because of Brooks’ current value on the market — $24 million AAV for a playoff-tested veteran wing that will be 32 once the extension kicks in might quietly be a bargain, which we’ll get into later — but more in line with what the Suns’ overall vision is as a play-in team. In an offseason that has been dictated by seismic movement from contenders repositioning themselves in a Knicks-centric world and an underlying lack of activity from bottom feeders hoping to latch on to losing, Phoenix appears to be interested in neither. 

Brooks’ extension is simply a continuation of continuity. The Suns have now secured guard Collin Gillespie (four years, $48 million), Mark Williams (three years, $38 million) and Jordan Goodwin (three years, $19 million) along with Brooks for the next iteration of the franchise. All four are on reasonable salaries that can be moved if an outside need arises. And in today’s erratic, inconsistent, ever-changing atmosphere, sticking to what you know is nothing to scoff at. 

Ring culture has consumed us and drives the bulk of league conversations, but there’s inherent value in remaining relevant. A plethora of teams would trade their fortunes for, say, the Portland Trail Blazers’ 2014-19 run. Over those six seasons, the franchise won 54, 51, 44, 41, 49 and 53 games. Outside of their Western Conference finals appearance in 2019 (a 4-0 sweep at the hands of Golden State), the Blazers were never considered a true threat. And that’s OK!

(There’s also no reason to think that Phoenix can’t be the next hotbed for another big move. The Suns’ current cap sheet, even while operating as a team over the first apron, is manageable. Head coach Jordan Ott is young, bright and has a clear-cut vision of how he operates. Yes, their asset war chest is shot — surrendering an unprotected 2033 first to acquire Miles Bridges was a real thing — but there’s enough young, interesting talent on the roster that would and should suffice in larger trades.)

Tying everything back to Brooks, who’s made a pretty penny for himself ever since being shoved out the door in Memphis, hitching his next few years to the Suns makes a ton of sense for both parties. Stepping into an elevated role, a huge usage spike all while maintaining a true shooting percentage in the ballpark of his Houston days, has paid dividends for a Suns team that needs answers not named Devin Booker in the half-court. If you agree with the idea that Brooks is a top-75ish offensive talent (54th in offensive WAR, 80th in DARKO), then pairing him over the long haul with Booker and Jalen Green should work in theory.
